analysis.one_liner: Eliminates Medicare's independent peer review system that checks the quality of care.
analysis.headline: A bill with zero cosponsors to eliminate Medicare's peer review system died in subcommittee without ever receiving a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would repeal Part B of title XI of the Social Security Act, wiping out the Medicare peer review system [S3]. That system uses outside Peer Review Organizations to independently check whether care paid for by Medicare — hospital stays, procedures, treatments — was medically necessary and met quality standards, and to investigate problems [S2]. The bill would shut that oversight down with no replacement [S2].
analysis.who_benefits: Hospitals and physicians would benefit most: no more outside reviewers examining whether admissions and treatments were medically necessary, which means less paperwork and less risk of denied claims or quality sanctions. Advocates of a smaller federal bureaucracy would also get a statutory oversight mandate fully repealed.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Hospitals and physicians facing Medicare quality review

how_it_helps.text: Hospitals and doctors would no longer face peer review organizations examining whether care was medically necessary or met quality standards, reducing administrative burden and the risk of denied payment or sanction.
Supporters of shrinking federal health bureaucracy would get an entire statutory oversight mandate repealed outright rather than trimmed or restructured.

analysis.who_pays: Medicare beneficiaries would lose the independent, system-wide check on whether their care was needed and properly performed, and would lose an outside body that can catch quality-of-care problems. Taxpayers would bear the risk of paying claims for care that was unnecessary or substandard, since no replacement oversight was proposed.

drawbacks.text: Beneficiaries would lose the only independent, program-wide review of whether hospital care was medically necessary and met quality standards, and the outside channel for catching quality-of-care problems.
Taxpayers would keep paying Medicare claims with no utilization review to screen out unnecessary care, raising the risk of paying for services that were not needed.
The bill offered no replacement safeguard — it simply repealed the mandate — so any quality or fraud problems that peer review now surfaces would go undetected.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The gain would be modest and one-sided: less paperwork and fewer external second-guesses for hospitals and doctors. The cost would fall on tens of millions of Medicare beneficiaries and taxpayers, who would lose the independent review that checks whether billed care was necessary and well performed, with nothing put in its place. The bill was a single sentence repealing the system, not a redesign.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced, referred to two committees and then to their health subcommittees, and nothing ever happened to it before that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. John J. Duncan Jr. introduced the bill on June 7, 1995, to repeal the part of the Social Security Act that establishes Medicare peer review.
No other member of the House signed on as a cosponsor.

The bill was referred to the Ways and Means and Commerce committees, then to the Health and Health and Environment subcommittees in June 1995; the record shows no hearings, no markup, and no vote afterward.
The 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997, and the bill died in subcommittee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Medicare beneficiaries came out ahead: the independent peer review system that checks whether their care was medically necessary and meets quality standards stayed in place.

for.name: Rep. John J. Duncan Jr.
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the Medicare peer review mandate; it drew no cosponsors.

against.name: House Ways and Means Subcommittee on Health
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on June 9, 1995 and never took the bill up.

against.name: House Commerce Subcommittee on Health and Environment
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on June 19, 1995 and never took the bill up.

sides.party_line_note: A one-sponsor bill with zero cosponsors that never reached a vote, so no partisan split can be measured.

industries.note: Peer review organizations examine whether hospital admissions and treatments paid for by Medicare were medically necessary and meet quality standards, and problems can lead to denied payment or sanctions. Eliminating the system would spare hospitals that scrutiny while leaving beneficiaries and taxpayers without the check.

Doctors treating Medicare patients would no longer have outside reviewers second-guessing the necessity or quality of the care they bill for, reducing administrative burden and payment risk at the cost of patient protection.

The bill repeals the statutory mandate that creates these organizations and their Medicare review work, ending their role outright. Their existence is the oversight itself, so their loss would have been the public's loss too.
